name: Tessa Nguyen

biography.name: Tessa Nguyen

background.family: Lives with her aunt, uncle, and two cousins; her mother works in another Texas city and calls most evenings.
background.finances: Family expenses are shared carefully; Tessa earns some spending money helping at a weekend food stall.
background.geography: A neighborhood near Galveston Bay, where drainage and weather change familiar walking routes.
background.cultureLanguages: English at school, Vietnamese at family meals; reads Vietnamese slowly.
background.school: Public school with a science club that meets inconsistently when transport and room access permit.
background.accessOpportunities: Has repeated experience recording local observations, a phone camera, borrowed reference books, and little access to specialized equipment.

timeline.story: Tessa noticed tiny shells caught in the cracks beside her aunt’s doorway and put them in a margarine tub. She forgot where several came from. Her uncle encouraged her to label the next batch, but she mostly wanted to look again after rain changed what appeared.

She watched ants avoid a wet strip on the pavement, then return by a different route. Her cousin said the ants were scared of water. Tessa repeated the observation the next afternoon and was bothered when nothing happened, although she did not yet know what to write down.

A teacher loaned her a magnifier. Tessa kept a notebook of leaves from three streets, drawing marks and recording where each leaf lay. She mixed up two specimens and crossed out a whole page. The teacher accepted the correction; Tessa still remembers it as a careless mistake.

She began recording puddle depth near the bus stop with a marked stick. After several weeks she noticed that her measuring position had shifted. She restarted, kept the old pages, and explained the difference when asked. She privately assumed a more capable person would have noticed sooner.

During a school investigation, Tessa recorded dates, repeated observations, and a possible alternative explanation that others omitted. Her group used her notes but chose another student to speak. She was relieved and disappointed together, then convinced herself that relief proved she did not understand the work well enough.

She compared shade and soil dampness in containers behind the apartment, using the same rough method over several months. A holiday interruption left a gap, which she marked instead of guessing. Her aunt praised the careful record; Tessa worried that household containers made the whole exercise too ordinary to count.

Tessa now has several years of imperfect observations and can explain why two sets should not be combined. She asks a teacher to check conclusions before saying them aloud, sometimes twice. She wants to investigate a new question independently but has not chosen one she considers worth other people’s time.
